chapters.title: Chapter 5: Central Banks in Crisis, and What Investors Learn

lessons.title: COVID 2020: When Central Banks Flooded the World With Liquidity

body.text: In March 2020, economies were deliberately shut down and markets fell faster than in 2008. Central banks responded with the largest and quickest support operation in history: rates to zero, unlimited bond buying, loans to almost anyone who needed them. It worked, in that the financial system never froze. It also planted the seeds of the inflation that arrived two years later.

children.text: This is the fourth crisis in this chapter, and the one where central banks acted fastest. It is also where the tools from Chapters 2 and 4 were used all at once: rate cuts, CRR cuts, targeted lending, QE and swap lines, within weeks of each other.

Indian markets did not wait for the lockdown. As the virus spread globally, the Nifty 50 fell from a January 2020 peak of about 12,430 to a low of 7,511 on 24 March 2020, the day after the nationwide lockdown was announced. Trading was halted twice that month when indices hit their 10% lower circuit limits: on 13 March and again on 23 March.

body.title: How Deep Was the Crash?
body.prompt: The Nifty 50 fell from about 12,430 in January 2020 to 7,511 on 24 March 2020. What was the percentage fall? Enter a negative number, rounded to one decimal place.
body.explanation: (7,511 − 12,430) ÷ 12,430 × 100 = about -39.6%. Roughly 40% of the index value disappeared in about two months, faster than the 2008 crash, which took over a year to fall further. Speed, not just depth, was what made March 2020 so frightening for policymakers.

body.text: A circuit breaker halts trading across the whole market when an index moves 10%, 15% or 20% in a day. Two market-wide halts in a single month had never happened in India before. The halts are designed to give investors time to think rather than panic, which is exactly what central banks were trying to achieve with their own announcements.

children.text: What the Fed Did, and How Fast

body.title: Three Weeks That Reset Global Policy

events.title: Emergency cut
events.description: The Fed cut rates by 50 basis points between scheduled meetings, its first emergency cut since 2008.

events.title: Rates to zero, QE restarts
events.description: On a Sunday, the Fed cut to 0% to 0.25% and announced $700 billion of bond purchases: $500 billion of Treasuries and $200 billion of mortgage securities.

events.title: Unlimited QE
events.description: The Fed pledged to buy Treasuries and mortgage securities in whatever amounts were needed, and for the first time began buying corporate debt.

events.title: A wall of liquidity
events.description: Dollar swap lines were widened, and the Fed balance sheet grew from about $4.2 trillion to over $7 trillion within months, on its way to the $8.96 trillion peak you saw in Chapter 4.

children.text: The RBI moved almost as fast, and reached for more tools than in any previous crisis.

body.title: How Far Did the Repo Rate Fall?
body.prompt: The repo rate was 5.15% before the pandemic measures and 4.00% after the May 2020 cut. How many basis points of cuts is that in total?
body.explanation: 5.15% minus 4.00% = 1.15 percentage points = 115 basis points, delivered in just two moves, on 27 March and 22 May 2020. For comparison, the entire 2025 easing cycle was 125 basis points spread across four decisions.

body.text: Notice the reverse repo cuts. By pushing the reverse repo rate to 3.35% while the repo rate sat at 4.00%, the RBI widened the corridor you studied in Chapter 2 to 65 basis points on the floor side. Money parked at the RBI earned much less than the policy rate, a deliberate nudge to make banks lend rather than hoard.

body.title: Measure the Lopsided Corridor
body.prompt: In May 2020 the repo rate was 4.00% and the reverse repo rate was 3.35%. How many basis points below the repo rate was the floor of the corridor?
body.explanation: 4.00% minus 3.35% = 0.65 percentage points = 65 basis points. Normally the floor sits 25 basis points below the repo rate, as the SDF does today. The unusually wide gap in 2020 was designed to penalise banks for parking cash instead of lending it.

children.text: Targeted Tools: Lending Where It Was Needed

markDefs.definition: Cheap long-term funding given by the RBI to banks on condition that the money is used to buy specific assets, such as corporate bonds, commercial paper or debentures of smaller companies.

children.text: Cutting rates helps only if credit actually flows. In 2020 the RBI leaned heavily on

, lending banks money at the repo rate for up to three years, provided they used it to buy corporate bonds and commercial paper. Later versions directed funds specifically towards smaller NBFCs and microfinance institutions, the firms most likely to be starved of credit.

body.title: Why Did the RBI Create a Facility for Mutual Funds?
body.question: On 27 April 2020, days after a fund house wound up six debt schemes, the RBI announced a ₹50,000 crore special liquidity facility for mutual funds. What problem was it solving?
options: Mutual funds needed capital to stay in business
Redemption pressure was forcing funds to sell bonds into a market with no buyers, risking a wider freeze in corporate debt
The RBI wanted to buy equity mutual fund units
The government had ordered the RBI to bail out investors
body.explanation: This was a liquidity problem, not a capital one. Investors were pulling money out of debt funds, and funds had to sell corporate bonds and commercial paper to pay them. With few buyers, prices were collapsing and the freeze threatened to spread. The RBI let banks borrow cheaply against such securities so they could buy from funds, restoring a functioning market. The lesson from Chapter 1 applies: a central bank fights panics by being the buyer or lender when everyone else steps back.

children.text: The support worked in the narrow sense that mattered most: banks kept functioning, companies kept borrowing, and markets recovered faster than almost anyone expected. As you saw in Chapter 4, the Nifty rose about 148% from its March 2020 low to its October 2021 peak, helped by record foreign inflows of ₹2.74 lakh crore in FY21.

body.text: The bill arrived later. Ultra-loose money everywhere, supply chains still broken and then the Russia-Ukraine war pushed global inflation to multi-decade highs in 2021 and 2022. The RBI eventually had to fail its own inflation target for three consecutive quarters, as you saw in Chapter 1, and raise the repo rate by 250 basis points. That is the subject of the next lesson.

children.text: The Moratorium: Relief With a Catch

For ordinary borrowers, the most visible measure was the EMI moratorium: permission to pause term loan repayments for three months, later extended to six. It was relief, but not forgiveness. Interest kept accruing on the outstanding balance during the pause, so the loan got bigger and either the EMI or the tenure rose afterwards.

body.title: What Does a Moratorium Really Cost?
body.prompt: Take a ₹30 lakh home loan at 8% a year. Interest for one month is the balance multiplied by 8% divided by 12. Roughly how much interest accrues on ₹30 lakh during a single skipped month, in ₹ thousand? Round to the nearest thousand.
body.explanation: ₹30,00,000 × 8% ÷ 12 = ₹20,000 of interest in that month. If you skip the EMI, that ₹20,000 is added to what you owe and starts earning interest itself. Over six months of moratorium the amount added runs to well over a lakh, which is why the RBI and courts later had to address the question of charging interest on that unpaid interest. A moratorium is a cash flow tool for people who genuinely cannot pay, not free money.

body.title: Go Deeper: Why the 2020 Response Was Different From 2008

children.text: In 2008 the crisis began inside the financial system: banks held bad assets and stopped trusting each other. Central banks had to repair the banks themselves, and the process took years.

In 2020 the banks were fine. The shock came from outside, as governments deliberately shut down economic activity to contain a virus. That made the central bank job different: keep credit flowing to fundamentally sound businesses through a temporary, if severe, interruption. It explains why support was so fast, so broad and so willing to reach beyond banks, to corporate bond markets, mutual funds and small lenders. It also explains why the recovery, once economies reopened, was far quicker than after 2008.

body.title: March 2020, and Your SIP
body.scenario: It is late March 2020. Your ₹10,000 monthly SIP in an equity index fund is down about 30%. Your employer has announced pay cuts, and you have about four months of expenses in a savings account. A colleague has stopped his SIP and moved everything to a fixed deposit. Another is borrowing to buy more stocks because prices are low.
body.prompt: What would you do with the SIP, the emergency fund and the temptation to borrow and invest?
body.modelAnswer: Start with the emergency fund, not the market. With pay cuts and job uncertainty, four months of expenses is thin, so the first priority is protecting and ideally increasing that buffer. If the SIP is affordable after that, continuing it is usually right: a monthly SIP buys more units when prices are low, which is exactly what produced strong returns for people who kept investing through 2020. Stopping the SIP after a 30% fall locks in the decline and misses the recovery, which in this case began within weeks. Borrowing to invest is the riskiest option of the three: leverage cuts both ways, and in March 2020 nobody knew how long the lockdowns would last or how deep the damage would be. As for watching central banks, the Fed cutting to zero, the RBI cutting rates and the sheer scale of liquidity announced were signals that policymakers would do whatever it took to keep the financial system intact. That reduces the risk of a total collapse; it does not guarantee any particular market level or timeline.

body.title: Learn From the Pandemic Response
steps: Check how many months of expenses your emergency fund would cover today
Look up your equity fund NAV in January 2020, March 2020 and one year later
If you took the 2020 moratorium on any loan, check how much your outstanding balance or tenure increased
Compare the repo rate of 4.00% in 2020 with today and note how much room the RBI has to cut in a future crisis
Read the RBI statement of 27 March 2020 and list how many different tools were used in one announcement

points: The Nifty fell about 40% from its January 2020 peak to 7,511 on 24 March 2020, with two market-wide circuit halts in one month.
The Fed cut to zero and launched unlimited QE within three weeks, expanding its balance sheet by trillions.
The RBI cut the repo rate by 115 basis points to 4.00%, cut CRR to 3%, and released about ₹1.37 lakh crore to banks.
Targeted tools mattered as much as rate cuts: TLTRO funding tied to corporate bond purchases, and a ₹50,000 crore facility for mutual funds.
The reverse repo was cut far below the repo rate, widening the corridor to 65 basis points to push banks to lend rather than park cash.
The response prevented a financial freeze and markets recovered quickly, but the flood of global liquidity contributed to the inflation surge that forced sharp tightening in 2022.
